title: jsonb, arrays, enums vs lookup tables vs CHECK
summary: jsonb suits attributes that really vary per row, arrays suit small lists read with the row; neither checks types or references. For a fixed set of values pick CHECK (simplest), an enum (ordered, compact, values never removable) or a lookup table (values that carry data or change often).

examples.title: json vs jsonb, querying attributes, and what jsonb doesn't check

annotations.note: jsonb parses the document once on input: whitespace, key order and duplicate keys are gone (only the last "a" survives). The docs advise jsonb for most applications; plain json only when the exact text must be kept.

The dividing line of this lesson. price exists for every product and is filtered, summed and constrained, so it is a column with a type. Tea has an origin, a cable has a length: those vary by category, so they go in jsonb.
-> returns jsonb (1000 is a JSON number), ->> returns text (Rize, not "Rize"). @> is containment and ? tests for a key; both can be served by a GIN index on attrs, which the JSON module covers.

A string where a number belongs, accepted without complaint. A CHECK such as jsonb_typeof(attrs -> 'weight_g') = 'number' would stop it; if you find yourself writing many such checks, the field wants to be a column.
SQLSTATE 22P02 at read time, far from the insert that caused it, and the whole report fails. This is the real cost of schemaless data: the validation you skipped on write is paid by every reader.

examples.title: Arrays: 1-based indexing, membership, unnest, and no foreign keys

annotations.note: text[] is an array of text. Declared sizes such as text[3] are accepted and ignored, per the docs. NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}' keeps "no tags" as an empty array, so code never has to tell NULL and {} apart.

Indexing starts at 1. tags[0] and tags[3] are NULL, not an error: like JS's undefined, unlike Python's IndexError or Go's panic. For the empty array, array_length(tags, 1) is NULL while cardinality(tags) is 0, so WHERE array_length(tags, 1) = 0 never matches.
'sql' = ANY (tags) reads naturally for one value; tags @> ARRAY['go', 'sql'] means "has all of these". A GIN index on tags can serve @> but not = ANY, so write tags @> ARRAY['sql'] on large tables.

unnest expands each row's array into rows, and the function in FROM can refer to the table before it. This is how arrays rejoin set-based SQL: as soon as you aggregate over elements, you are treating them as rows.

'golang' next to 'go' is now a second tag, and nothing can stop it: a foreign key can't point into an array. The docs' own tip: arrays are not sets, and searching for elements can be a sign of misdesign. When tags need integrity or data of their own, use a junction table.

examples.title: One status, three designs: enum, lookup table, CHECK

annotations.note: An enum is a type: 4 bytes per value, labels case-sensitive, and two different enum types can't even be compared. Values can be added and renamed, but never removed or reordered without recreating the type.
A lookup table holds the values as rows. With the code itself as the primary key, tickets.as_lookup stays readable without a join; the join is only needed for the label and position.
A CHECK keeps the column plain text and the allowed list in the table's definition. Easiest to read, but only this table knows the list.

enum_order follows the declaration: open, in_progress, done. text_order is alphabetical: done, in_progress, open. If "sort by status" should mean workflow order, text needs a CASE or a position column.
Labels and order are data: translating a label or moving a status is an UPDATE, not a migration. Neither an enum nor a CHECK can attach a Turkish label to a value.

In a migration the type already exists, and the docs' rule applies: a value added inside a transaction block can't be used until that transaction commits. (This sandbox created the type in the same transaction, a case where Postgres allows the new value at once.)
Changing a CHECK means dropping and re-adding it, and the new one scans every row under an exclusive lock. On a large table, add it NOT VALID and validate separately, as the ALTER TABLE lesson shows.
SQLSTATE 23503: rows still say 'open'. Retiring a lookup value is explicit (migrate the rows, or add an active flag); for an enum there is no statement for it at all.

use_cases: jsonb: per-category product attributes, per-integration settings, raw webhook payloads kept for replay
arrays: tags or labels read and written with their row, small value lists without an identity of their own
CHECK (x IN ...): short, stable lists owned by one table
enum: stable, ordered states shared by several tables (severity, workflow stage)
lookup table: values with labels, translations, sort order or flags, or values that change at business speed
strengths: jsonb gives per-row flexibility without an entity-attribute-value table, and GIN indexes make @> and ? fast
An array keeps a short list inside the row: one read, no join, and GIN-indexable containment
enum values are 4 bytes, typo-proof, and sort in a meaningful order
A lookup table is the only option where values carry data and change with DML instead of DDL
weaknesses: Nothing inside jsonb or an array is type-checked or reference-checked unless you add CHECK constraints
Changing one key or element writes a new version of the whole row and locks it, which the docs flag for large documents
Enum values can't be removed or reordered without recreating the type, and an added value can't be used before it commits
A lookup table costs a foreign-key check on every write and a join for every label

pitfalls.title: jsonb for core fields
pitfalls.detail: Fields that every row has and that queries filter, join or sum on lose types, NOT NULL, foreign keys and planner statistics inside jsonb.
pitfalls.good: price numeric(12, 2) NOT NULL as a column; jsonb for the leftovers

pitfalls.title: Arrays of foreign keys
pitfalls.detail: author_ids int[] can't be checked against authors, and deleting an author leaves dangling ids. A junction table with two foreign keys can.
pitfalls.good: article_authors (article_id REFERENCES articles, author_id REFERENCES authors, PRIMARY KEY (article_id, author_id))

pitfalls.title: Testing an empty array with array_length
pitfalls.detail: array_length of an empty array is NULL, so the comparison is never true.

pitfalls.title: Adding an enum value and using it in one migration
pitfalls.detail: Migration tools usually wrap each migration in a transaction; the new value can't be used before ALTER TYPE commits. Put ADD VALUE and the UPDATE that uses it in separate migrations.

pitfalls.title: Comparing or grouping json values
pitfalls.detail: The json type has no equality operator, so =, DISTINCT and GROUP BY on json fail with 'operator does not exist: json = json'. jsonb has one.

pitfalls.title: Appending a literal to an array with ||
pitfalls.detail: tags || 'golang' reads the literal as an array and fails with malformed array literal. Use array_append(tags, 'golang') or ARRAY['golang'].

quiz.q: An object in a jsonb input has the same key twice. What is stored?
options: Only the last value for that key
quiz.why: jsonb doesn't keep duplicate keys; only the last value is kept. (json keeps the exact text, duplicates included.)

quiz.q: tags is text[] holding {go,sql}. What is tags[0]?
quiz.why: Arrays are 1-based and an out-of-bounds subscript returns NULL instead of raising an error.

quiz.q: Ticket statuses need a Turkish label each, and support staff add new ones every month. Which design fits?
options: Lookup table plus a foreign key
quiz.why: Only a lookup table lets values carry data (the label) and be added or retired with plain DML.

quiz.q: Why can't one migration transaction run ALTER TYPE status ADD VALUE 'archived' and then set rows to 'archived'?
options: A new enum value can't be used until the ALTER TYPE commits
ADD VALUE is not allowed in a transaction block
quiz.why: Since PostgreSQL 12 ADD VALUE may run in a transaction block, but the docs say the new value can't be used until the transaction has committed.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: ALTER TYPE (adding enum values)

body:
## Concept

Relational columns give you types, constraints and statistics per field. Three features
relax that, each for a specific shape of data:

- **`jsonb`**: a parsed JSON document per row, for attributes that differ from row to
  row. Queryable (`->`, `->>`, `@>`, `?`) and indexable, but nothing inside is checked.
- **Arrays** (`text[]`, `int[]`): an ordered list inside the row, for small lists you
  read and write with it. 1-based, and no foreign keys into them.
- **A fixed set of values** (a status, a severity) can be declared three ways: a
  `CHECK (x IN (...))` on a text column, an `enum` type, or a lookup table referenced by
  a foreign key. They differ in what changing the set costs.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **TypeScript:** `'open' | 'in_progress' | 'done'` is the same idea as an enum or a CHECK,
  enforced at a different layer; a `jsonb` column is `Record<string, unknown>` and needs
  validating (zod) when it comes back, exactly like a `fetch` response.
- **Java:** Java enums are ordered like Postgres enums, but Java enums can carry fields.
  Postgres enums can't; that's what the lookup table is for.
- **Go:** Go has no enum type, only typed constants, so the database enum is stricter than
  your Go code. `jsonb` maps naturally to `json.RawMessage` or a struct via
  `encoding/json`.
- **Python/JS:** arrays here start at 1, and out-of-range reads return NULL, not an
  `IndexError`.
- **Document databases:** `jsonb` gives you a document per column inside a relational row,
  so you can keep transactions, joins and constraints for everything that is stable.

## Design notes

Structured where it's stable, JSON where it isn't. If every row has the field, or you
filter, join or sum on it, it is a column. `jsonb` earns its place for the long tail of
optional attributes and for payloads you store as received. The docs also suggest keeping
documents to a predictable structure and a manageable size, since every update rewrites
and locks the whole row.

Arrays are a denormalization: fine for tags that are just strings, wrong as soon as the
elements are references to other rows or need their own data.

For value sets, start with CHECK: it's plain text, visible in the table definition, and
changing it is ordinary DDL. Choose an enum when the order matters and the set is stable
across many tables. Choose a lookup table when values carry data (labels, translations,
positions, an active flag) or when people outside engineering add them.

files.examples/01_jsonb.sql:
-- json keeps the text you typed; jsonb parses it: keys reordered,
-- duplicates dropped (the last one wins).
SELECT '{"b": 1, "a": 2, "a": 3}'::json  AS as_json,
       '{"b": 1, "a": 2, "a": 3}'::jsonb AS as_jsonb;

CREATE TABLE products (
  sku   text PRIMARY KEY,
  name  text NOT NULL,
  price numeric(10, 2) NOT NULL,     -- every product has one: a real column
  attrs jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'  -- differs per category: jsonb
);

INSERT INTO products VALUES
  ('tea-rize', 'Rize çayı',   249.90, '{"origin": "Rize", "weight_g": 1000}'),
  ('tea-earl', 'Earl Grey',   189.50, '{"origin": "Sri Lanka", "weight_g": 250, "organic": true}'),
  ('usb-c',    'USB-C kablo', 129.00, '{"length_m": 2, "watts": 100}');

-- -> returns jsonb, ->> returns text. @> asks "does attrs contain this
-- document?", ? asks "does it have this key?".
SELECT sku, attrs -> 'weight_g' AS weight_json, attrs ->> 'origin' AS origin
FROM products
WHERE attrs @> '{"origin": "Rize"}' OR attrs ? 'organic'
ORDER BY sku;

-- Nothing checks the shape of a jsonb value, so this insert succeeds...
INSERT INTO products VALUES
  ('tea-green', 'Yeşil çay', 99.00, '{"origin": "Rize", "weight_g": "yarım kilo"}');

-- ...and the mistake surfaces later, in somebody else's report.
SELECT sum((attrs ->> 'weight_g')::int) AS total_tea_grams
FROM products
WHERE sku LIKE 'tea-%';
files.examples/02_arrays.sql:
CREATE TABLE articles (
  id    int    PRIMARY KEY,
  title text   NOT NULL,
  tags  text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'
);

INSERT INTO articles VALUES
  (1, 'Goroutines in practice', ARRAY['go', 'concurrency']),
  (2, 'timestamptz explained',  ARRAY['sql', 'time']),
  (3, 'pgx and transactions',   ARRAY['go', 'sql']),
  (4, 'Draft',                  '{}');

-- Arrays are 1-based, and reading outside the bounds yields NULL, not an
-- error. For an empty array, array_length() is NULL and cardinality() is 0.
SELECT id, tags[1] AS first, tags[0] AS index_zero, tags[3] AS past_end,
       array_length(tags, 1) AS array_length, cardinality(tags) AS cardinality
FROM articles
ORDER BY id;

-- Membership: = ANY for one value, @> for "contains all of these".
SELECT id, title FROM articles WHERE 'sql' = ANY (tags) ORDER BY id;
SELECT id, title FROM articles WHERE tags @> ARRAY['go', 'sql'] ORDER BY id;

-- unnest turns an array back into rows: articles per tag.
SELECT tag, count(*) AS articles
FROM articles, unnest(tags) AS tag
GROUP BY tag
ORDER BY tag;

-- No foreign key reaches inside an array, so a typo is stored happily.
UPDATE articles SET tags = array_append(tags, 'golang') WHERE id = 1
RETURNING id, tags;
